items.title: Rosa Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress
items.claim: Rosa Parks's December 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat is often told as a spontaneous act. What was her actual background?

options.text: She had no prior political involvement and acted purely on impulse
She was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School months earlier
She was a paid organiser sent specifically to provoke an arrest
She was a member of the Communist Party, which is why she was arrested

items.reveal:
Parks had been Montgomery NAACP secretary since 1943. In summer 1955 she attended a workshop at Highlander Folk School in Tennessee on desegregation strategy. She was also not the first to refuse — Claudette Colvin had done the same in March 1955 but was 15, pregnant, and considered unsuitable as a test case by the NAACP.

Parks later wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
items.why: The 'tired seamstress' story makes civil rights feel like an accident of individual virtue. The actual story is one of organised, strategic activism — which is harder to teach but truer.

items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: Charles I lost the Civil War partly because he was a poor commander
items.claim: What contributed to Charles I's defeat (1642-1646) beyond political 'tyranny'?

options.text: Parliamentary forces always vastly outnumbered the king's

Parliament held London (wealth, manpower), the navy, and after 1645 the New Model Army; Charles repeatedly failed to coordinate his commanders and missed strategic opportunities like marching on London after Edgehill
The Scots refused to fight on either side
Charles was killed in battle at Naseby

items.reveal_title: The man, not just the cause
items.reveal:
After the indecisive Edgehill (October 1642), Charles failed to march on London while it was undefended. The Solemn League and Covenant (1643) brought Scottish forces in on Parliament's side. The New Model Army (formed 1645) under Fairfax and Cromwell was the first national professional army.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646; they handed him to Parliament. His attempts to negotiate while plotting a second war (the 'Engagement' with the Scots, 1647) destroyed any remaining trust and led to his trial.
items.why: Wars are won by armies, logistics and leadership — not just by who has the better political argument. Charles's strategic failures are often glossed over in the rush to debate 'tyranny vs liberty'.
